I am 54 years old and have farmed these flat lands of Quzhou County my whole life. I have no schooling, but I know this soil and this weather. Here on the North China Plain, our family holds about six mu of good cropland, and I also keep a small corner near the house for vegetables for our own table. This year, just like every year, I will follow the double-cropping rotation because that is what this land and the short growing season allow. 

In mid-October I will sow winter wheat. I will buy improved seed from the county supply station — probably Jimai or something similar — because it stands up to wind and gives a steady harvest. Before sowing I will run the rotary tiller to break up the stubble left from the maize. For fertilizer, I will spread compound fertilizer giving about 15 kg of nitrogen per mu, plus phosphate and a little potash. The wheat will need four irrigations: the overwintering water before the deep cold, the jointing water in spring, the heading water, and one more at grain filling. I will spray three times for aphids and powdery mildew, because if you skip this the yield drops badly.

As soon as the wheat comes off in early June, I will plant summer maize without delay. I will use Zhengdan 958 hybrid seed — everyone around here plants it because it is reliable and the county buyers know it. I will not deep-plough; I will plant directly into the wheat stubble with no-tillage to save time before the summer rains come. The maize needs more nitrogen than wheat, about 17 kg per mu, and I will irrigate twice during the summer if the drought is strong. Two pesticide sprays should keep the corn borer away. If the weather cooperates I expect about 500 kg per mu from the wheat and 550 kg per mu from the maize. The grain prices have been steady enough, so this plan should cover the cost of seeds and chemicals and still leave food and cash for the family.
